title: The Fruit-Seller Receives a Gift of Jewels
story:
In those days Krishna was still small enough to be carried, and his days in Gokula were full of play. He danced whenever the cowherd women clapped and coaxed him to dance. When his father asked, he would fetch the stool and the weights and the wooden sandals and carry them, pleased to be of use. To anyone with eyes to see, the Lord of all things was going about the lanes of a cowherd village like an ordinary child, happy to be asked, happy to serve. He was learning the weight of a stool in his arms the way any child learns it, and the women of the house laughed to see him trot off at an errand and come back beaming.

One morning a fruit-seller came through the lane, a woman with a basket of fruit and a voice that carried down the street. Come, buy fruits! Sweet fruits! she called. The cry rolled ahead of her through the little village, and heads turned at the sound of it.

Krishna heard the cry and hurried at once. He snatched up a fistful of grain to barter — grain was what a village that kept no coins gave and took — and ran toward the fruit-seller, eager for the trade. He had seen the fruit-seller's trade before, baskets carried from lane to lane, and the exchange was a small boy's idea of the world's business: you give, you get, everybody is pleased.

But his hands were small, and his eagerness was greater than his grip. Before he reached the woman, the grain began to run out through his fingers and spill onto the ground, a thin white trail marking where he had run. By the time he stood before her, his two fists were nearly empty.

The fruit-seller looked down at the child — at the grain scattered in the dust and the two small, empty hands held up to her — and her heart turned over. She did not scold him. She laughed, softly, and bent down and began to fill his small hands with fruit, heaping them with what she carried, until no more would stay. Whatever anyone else might have done with an empty-handed bargainer, she did the one thing that costs nothing and means everything: she gave.

And then she saw her basket.

Where her fruit had been, the basket now gleamed. In place of the fruit she had emptied into the child's hands, it was full to the brim with jewels — gems that caught the morning light and threw it back in every colour. The fruit was gone, and in its place shone a treasure beyond anything her life of selling fruit had ever held. The basket that had weighed in her arms like a day's honest work now weighed like a king's ransom.

She stood still, the heavy basket in her hands, and looked from the jewels to the small boy before her, and back again. She understood, in that moment, that she had not been selling fruit to a child at all. She had been giving it, without knowing, to the one who gives everything back a hundredfold.

But she said nothing of what she understood. She only looked at him, and he looked back at her — a child with his arms full of fruit, and a woman with her basket full of light.
reflection: The exchange turns on a small, human generosity: the woman is not asked for anything but fruit, and she gives it to a child who has already dropped his payment. What comes back is beyond measure, because grace answers the open hand.
hero_scene: A fruit-seller woman stares in wonder at her basket now brimming with gleaming jewels, while small Krishna stands before her with his arms heaped full of fruit and grain scattered in the dust behind him.

a woman's basket overflowing with jewels
